visual.headline:
AGILE TESTING
DOCUMENTS THAT HELP
visual.title: Agile Testing Documentation | Test Cases, Defects & Traceability | Episode 9
visual.question: Can another person reproduce the result?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.text: Agile values useful documentation, not the elimination of documentation. We will examine stories, criteria, cases, defects, charters and traceability. Imagine joining a team just before release. The invoice feature looks finished, but nobody can explain which account-isolation checks ran or which build contains the last fix. More documents would not automatically solve the problem. Useful artifacts would connect the customer need, expected behavior and evidence. Agile values working software, while still recognizing that documentation can support collaboration and decisions. In this lesson we create a small, connected set of artifacts for a monthly invoice download. Every artifact should answer a practical question for someone who needs to understand, verify, operate or change the product.

chapters.title: Stories and criteria
chapters.text: A customer wants to download a monthly invoice. Clarify completed billing periods, P D F output and account ownership. Acceptance criteria translate the need into verifiable outcomes. Write the user story in terms of the customer goal: a customer wants to download a monthly invoice to keep a record of charges. Then clarify the acceptance criteria. Only completed billing periods are available, the output is a readable P D F, and customers can access only their own invoices. Add an example of a month with no charge if the business needs it. Criteria should describe observable outcomes rather than merely repeat interface labels. A story that says there is a Download button is incomplete if it never explains which document the button must retrieve or who is allowed to retrieve it.

chapters.title: Test cases
chapters.text: A test case can specify ID, objective, precondition, action and expected result. For invoice downloads, verify that an authenticated customer downloads the correct P D F. Use detailed cases for high-risk work and checklists where sufficient. Create one test case with enough detail for its risk. Its identifier is INV zero one. The precondition is a synthetic customer with a completed billing period and a known invoice. The action is to request that period's download. The expected result is the correct P D F with the agreed account and charge information. Record the environment and build when executing it. A second test should investigate access to another synthetic customer's invoice. Detailed steps are useful where precision matters, but a simple low-risk visual check may only need a checklist. Match the detail to the reader's need and the consequences of ambiguity.

chapters.title: Defect reports
chapters.text: An invoice ID modification that exposes another customer’s file is a serious authorization issue. Record environment, steps, expected and actual behavior, and sanitized evidence. Avoid exposing sensitive customer data. Suppose modifying the invoice identifier returns another account's document. Write a defect that explains the authorization failure without exposing real customer information. Include the environment, synthetic account relationship, reproduction steps and observed result. State the expected denial and attach sanitized evidence. Link the affected requirement and test. Avoid putting access tokens or confidential invoices in a broadly shared ticket. The report should help the team reproduce and prioritize the problem, not create a second exposure. After the fix, retain enough retest evidence to show which build was checked and what outcome was observed.

chapters.title: Plans and charters
chapters.text: A lightweight strategy documents scope, risks, environments, responsibilities and automation. An exploratory charter might focus on invoice downloads across roles and billing periods. Capture observations afterward. A one-page strategy can describe scope, important risks, environments, responsibilities and the mix of automated and human checks. For this feature, highlight account isolation, document accuracy and availability. Add an exploratory charter: investigate invoice access across roles and billing periods using synthetic accounts. A charter sets a mission while leaving room to follow discoveries. After the session, capture what was covered, what was found and what remains uncertain. This is more useful than a long plan copied from an unrelated project that nobody updates or uses when making a release decision.

chapters.title: Traceability
chapters.text: Link authorization requirements to tests, defects, fixes and retest evidence. This helps teams demonstrate coverage, especially in regulated environments, without unnecessary bureaucracy. Traceability can be lightweight. Connect the account-ownership rule to the unauthorized-download check. Link the failing result to the defect, then the fix and retest. Someone reviewing release readiness can follow that chain and understand why the risk is considered addressed. The same principle applies to automated results: retain the build and relevant report rather than only a screenshot of a green badge. Avoid maintaining multiple disconnected copies of the same relationship in spreadsheets and tickets. A small set of current links is easier to trust than a large matrix that stopped reflecting the product several sprints ago.

chapters.title: Practical document set
chapters.text: Maintain stories, criteria, risk strategy, important tests, defect reports, automated results and relevant release notes. Keep artifacts accessible and current. Decide what to keep current. Stories and criteria describe the agreed behavior. Important tests preserve repeatable checks. Defect reports record actionable failures. Automated reports show what ran on a build. Operational notes explain relevant deployment or support concerns. Release notes communicate changes to their intended audience. Each artifact has a different reader and lifespan. When behavior changes, identify which artifacts now contain an obsolete rule. Documentation debt grows when old expectations remain easy to find but hard to distinguish from current guidance. Prefer concise material with clear ownership and a visible relationship to the implementation.

chapters.title: Worked example
chapters.text: For your exercise, create a miniature evidence chain for the invoice authorization defect. Write one criterion, one negative test, a concise defect title and a retest note. The criterion restricts downloads to the owning customer. The test attempts access from a different synthetic account. The defect states that the file was returned. The retest note identifies the fixed build and the observed denial. Explain why a screenshot alone would be insufficient if it omitted the account context and build. Useful documentation allows another person to reconstruct the decision without needing the original tester to explain every missing detail.

chapters.title: A closer look
chapters.text: Review a bad test case: click Download and verify the invoice is correct. It leaves correctness undefined. Improve it by naming the synthetic account, billing period, expected document identity and important fields. Record which build and environment were used. Now another tester can tell whether the file belongs to the right account and period, rather than simply confirming that a P D F opened. Do not add irrelevant detail, such as every pointer movement, if it does not help reproducibility. Precision should serve the risk and the reader. A concise test with an observable expected result can be more useful than pages of mechanical steps with an ambiguous conclusion.

chapters.title: Verify the outcome
chapters.text: Documentation also needs maintenance when the product changes. Suppose invoices become available on the first business day after a billing period instead of immediately at its end. Update the acceptance examples, automated expectations, relevant support guidance and any checks that rely on the previous availability rule. Record the change where the team will look for current behavior. An obsolete test can create noise, while an obsolete customer-facing explanation can create confusion. Assign ownership to the artifact that matters and remove redundant copies where possible. Keeping a small set of documents current is usually more useful than creating a large collection whose readers cannot identify the authoritative version.

chapters.title: Recap
chapters.text: Documentation should help teams understand and decide. Knowledge check: what details make a defect reproducible? visual.headline:
KANBAN TESTING
FIX THE BOTTLENECK
visual.title: Kanban for Software Testing | WIP Limits & Flow Metrics | Episode 10
visual.question: Why is the Testing queue always full?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.text: Kanban supports teams that receive work continuously, including support and maintenance operations. It makes flow visible and supports delivery predictability. Picture a support team receiving authentication failures, dashboard requests and small mobile fixes throughout the day. Work arrives continuously, so the team needs visibility into what is active, what is waiting and what is becoming old. Kanban helps the team define and improve that flow. A board is part of the approach, but the board alone cannot solve capacity problems. The team also needs explicit policies, limits and regular inspection. We will follow five fictional requests and show how testing contributes to finishing valuable work rather than becoming an invisible queue near the end.

chapters.title: Visual workflow
chapters.text: Represent requests as cards moving through Backlog, Ready, Development, Testing and Done. The board exposes current status and queues. Define the workflow before drawing columns. Backlog contains possible work, Ready contains requests that meet the team's entry policy, Development contains active implementation, Testing contains active or queued verification, and Done meets the agreed completion policy. These are illustrative choices, not required Kanban column names. Make the start and finish points explicit because metrics depend on them. A blocked item should remain visible in the system with its blocker, rather than being moved somewhere that hides its age. The board should represent how work actually flows, including waiting that the team may otherwise overlook.

chapters.title: WIP limits
chapters.text: Limit active work to reduce context switching. If Testing has three items and its limit is three, finish or unblock existing work before pulling more. Adjust limits to actual capacity. Suppose Testing has a limit of three items and already contains three. Two depend on an unavailable environment, while the third needs a small fix. Starting several more features increases active work without increasing finished value. The team might help restore the environment and pair on the small fix. When an item finishes, capacity becomes available to pull more. A limit is a policy that encourages this discussion; it is not a magic number copied from another team. Review whether the chosen limits support collaboration and manageable flow, then adjust through explicit experiments rather than quietly ignoring them.

chapters.title: Flow metrics
chapters.text: Lead time is measured from a defined request or commitment point to completion; cycle time is measured from the start of work to completion. Agree on boundaries before comparing results. Use timestamps to explain flow measures. A request arrives Monday, becomes active Wednesday and finishes Friday. If the team measures request-to-finish time, that includes the waiting before Wednesday. If its cycle-time boundary starts when work becomes active, the earlier waiting is outside that measure. State whether you use elapsed calendar time or working time. The current Kanban Guide emphasizes work in progress, throughput, work item age and cycle time as flow metrics. Lead time is also used in practice, with boundaries that must be defined. Unlabelled numbers from different workflows should not be compared as though they describe the same thing.

chapters.title: Bottlenecks
chapters.text: A growing Testing queue may indicate environment issues, oversized stories, weak upstream tests or capacity constraints. Improve overall flow before assuming headcount is the only solution. A constantly full Testing column is a signal, not a diagnosis. The cause could be unstable environments, large batches, missing acceptance criteria, poor testability or a capacity mismatch. Examine individual items and their waiting time before proposing a solution. If every item waits for the same shared account, creating isolated data may help more than adding another dashboard. If large changes arrive in batches, smaller slices and earlier checks may reduce the queue. The objective is better flow through the whole system, so moving a bottleneck to another column without improving completion does not establish success.

chapters.title: Classes of service
chapters.text: Differentiate critical incidents, standard enhancements and fixed-date commitments with clear policies. Too many urgent tickets undermine prioritization. Classes of service make tradeoffs explicit when the team chooses to use them. A production authentication outage may qualify for expedited handling under an agreed policy. A normal dashboard enhancement follows standard capacity. A contractual deadline may require a fixed-date policy. These are complementary practices, not mandatory labels for every Kanban system. Too many expedited items undermine predictability because ordinary work is repeatedly interrupted. Define who can invoke an urgent policy, what evidence is needed and how interrupted work remains visible. Priority should reflect consequences and commitments rather than whoever asks most loudly.

chapters.title: Maintenance example
chapters.text: A team supporting a website, dashboard and mobile app receives five requests. A production authentication issue receives expedited attention while other items follow available capacity and testing checks. Walk through the five requests. One is an active production login failure, two are routine dashboard improvements, one is a mobile display defect and one is a reporting change with a future commitment. Assess the login incident first because customers cannot access the service. Apply the agreed urgent policy and make the interruption visible. Keep the other items ordered according to value, risk and capacity. After the incident fix, verify the important login journeys and capture a regression check where useful. Then inspect the cause so that the team learns from the interruption instead of simply celebrating a fast ticket closure.

chapters.title: Worked example
chapters.text: For your exercise, investigate a Testing queue that has remained full for a week. Record each item's age, its blocker and the work needed to finish it. Choose one action that could reduce waiting across several items, such as restoring a shared dependency or preparing independent test accounts. Decide how you will observe whether the action improves completion. Do not assume the busiest-looking column is the only problem; it may reflect issues upstream. A strong Kanban discussion connects visible work, explicit policies and evidence about flow to a practical experiment that the team can inspect.

chapters.title: A closer look
chapters.text: Work item age is especially useful before work finishes. Suppose three testing items are active: one started today, one three days ago and one nine days ago. A completed-item average will not explain the oldest item's current risk because it has not finished yet. Inspect why it is aging. Perhaps it depends on a supplier response or contains a much larger scope than the others. Make the blocker and next action visible. Historical cycle-time data can help the team discuss expectations, but it should not be treated as a guarantee for every request. Different work types and changed conditions can alter what a reasonable expectation looks like.

chapters.title: Verify the outcome
chapters.text: Avoid maximizing individual utilization at the expense of flow. If developers begin more features whenever testing waits, the board may show impressive activity while customers receive few completed changes. Helping finish an older item can be more valuable than starting another. That might mean clarifying a rule, reducing a change's scope, improving testability or investigating a failing integration together. Measure whether completed throughput and waiting improve under the experiment. A work in progress limit should encourage this system-level conversation. It should not become a rigid excuse to leave a colleague blocked while everyone else starts work that will soon join the same queue.

chapters.title: Recap
chapters.text: Kanban improves transparency and flow. Knowledge check: what should be investigated when the Testing column is consistently full? visual.headline:
AGILE TESTING
TOOLS & AUTOMATION
visual.title: Agile Testing Tools & Automation | API, Playwright & CI/CD | Episode 11
visual.question: What does a green build actually prove?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.text: Tools help Agile teams obtain reliable feedback quickly. We cover issue tracking, A P I tests, browser and mobile automation, performance, security and continuous integration and delivery. Imagine a team with many testing products but slow feedback and frequent escaped payment defects. More tools would not automatically fix the problem. The team must first identify what evidence it needs and where a tool can produce it reliably. In this lesson, connect tools to activities: tracking helps communicate work, A P I clients inspect service behavior, browser and mobile frameworks repeat journeys, performance tools explore load and CI coordinates checks. Product interfaces change over time, so focus on the underlying workflow. A good toolchain makes important outcomes easier to investigate and failures easier to understand.

chapters.title: Issue tracking
chapters.text: Use Jira, Azure DevOps or GitHub Issues to connect stories, defects and verification work. For a login lockout defect, record evidence, link the story and retest the fix. For a login-lockout defect, use an issue tracker to connect the affected story, the observed failure and the verification work. Include the build, synthetic account setup and expected policy. An issue tracker can help make responsibility and status visible, but it does not determine whether the policy is correct. Avoid copying sensitive credentials into a ticket. When the fix is ready, record the retest outcome and relevant regression results. Whether the team uses Jira, Azure DevOps or GitHub Issues, the important relationship is the same: expectation, evidence, defect, fix and verification remain understandable together.

chapters.title: API testing
chapters.text: Postman can send requests and inspect status codes, payloads and authentication behavior. Test valid login, invalid login, missing fields and expired tokens against the agreed A P I specification. Use an A P I client to send a fictional login request in a test environment. Check a valid account, an incorrect password, missing required fields and an expired token where the contract defines that behavior. Inspect the status, response body and resulting state. The exact expected status codes must come from the A P I specification; do not assume every product uses identical codes. A successful response alone does not prove permissions are correct. Follow it with an authorized operation and an operation the account must not perform. Use synthetic secrets and keep environment files with credentials out of shared reports.

chapters.title: Web and mobile automation
chapters.text: Selenium and Playwright can automate web journeys; Appium supports mobile automation. Use stable selectors, independent data and meaningful assertions to avoid fragile scripts. A browser check can visit the login page, fill clearly identified controls, submit and verify a meaningful signed-in outcome. Prefer user-facing locators or stable test identifiers over fragile page coordinates. Arrange independent data so one failed test does not break the next. For mobile, choose a framework compatible with the application and required platforms; Appium is one option. Decide which journeys justify the cost of end-to-end execution. Repeating every arithmetic rule through a full browser session makes feedback slower and can introduce unrelated failure points that a focused lower-level check avoids.

chapters.title: Performance and security
chapters.text: JMeter and k6 can help measure response time, throughput and error rates under load. OWASP ZAP can help discover some web vulnerabilities. No scanner proves complete security. For performance work, define a realistic scenario and an agreed target before running a tool such as k6 or JMeter. Track errors and response-time distributions alongside throughput. Averages can hide slow experiences for some requests. Security tools such as OWASP ZAP can identify some classes of web issues in an authorized environment, but a scan is not a complete security assessment. Business-rule abuse and access-control mistakes may require targeted investigation. Tool output is a starting point for interpretation. Confirm important findings and explain the conditions under which a measurement or observation was collected.
chapters.direction: Performance charts and security scan summary.

chapters.title: Continuous integration
chapters.text: A code commit triggers build, unit tests, integration tests and potentially deployment to a test environment followed by end-to-end checks. Jenkins and GitHub Actions can orchestrate these steps. A CI pipeline can begin when a commit is pushed. Build the application, run focused unit checks, run integration checks and deploy to an isolated test environment if appropriate. Then execute a smaller set of critical end-to-end journeys. Jenkins and GitHub Actions can orchestrate such stages, while actual capabilities depend on the configured project. When a check fails, retain useful logs and sanitized artifacts. Keep fast feedback close to the change, and avoid making every commit wait for a long experiment that could run at another appropriate point. The pipeline should provide reliable signals rather than merely execute many commands.

chapters.title: Automation strategy
chapters.text: Prioritize authentication, permissions, billing and payments. Put many business-rule checks at unit and A P I layers, retain a smaller number of critical end-to-end checks and review flaky tests regularly. Prioritize automation by risk, repeatability and maintenance cost. Stable billing calculations often suit focused unit tests. Service contracts suit A P I and integration checks. A small number of critical customer journeys suit browser or mobile checks. Human exploration remains valuable for new behavior and unexpected interactions. Review flaky tests because a check that randomly fails can teach people to ignore real failures. A retry may help diagnose instability, but it should not erase the evidence. Assign ownership to important checks and remove obsolete expectations when product behavior intentionally changes.

chapters.title: Worked example
chapters.text: Your exercise is to design a toolchain for a subscription checkout change. Identify one tracking artifact, one calculation check, one A P I scenario and one end-to-end journey. Add a controlled performance question if traffic is a material risk. Explain where each check runs and what a failure would tell the team. For example, verify fee arithmetic quickly, verify payment-state transitions at the A P I layer and verify one complete sandbox purchase through the interface. This plan produces clearer feedback than automating every rule only through the browser, because failures can be investigated closer to the component and risk involved.

chapters.title: A closer look
chapters.text: Read a failed automated check as evidence, not a verdict. A browser timeout might mean the application was slow, the selector was wrong, the environment was unavailable or the test waited for the wrong event. Preserve the trace, request information and relevant screenshot, then investigate. A blind rerun that passes does not explain the first failure. Repeatedly ignoring intermittent failures reduces confidence in the suite. Classify the cause and improve the check or product as appropriate. Reliable automation includes ownership of the feedback loop, not just the initial effort of recording a sequence of actions in a tool.

chapters.title: Verify the outcome
chapters.text: Consider a practical pipeline budget. Focused calculation checks can run frequently because they are fast and isolated. A P I and integration checks add evidence about service boundaries. A small critical browser suite checks complete customer journeys. Longer performance experiments can run when an appropriate environment and workload are available. The exact cadence depends on risk and delivery needs; there is no universal schedule. Record what each stage covers and what it omits. This lets the team interpret a green build honestly and decide when additional human investigation or specialized testing is needed before a significant release.

chapters.title: Recap
chapters.text: Choose tools to support quality risks and team workflow. Knowledge check: why is it inefficient to test every rule only through browser automation? visual.headline:
AGILE TESTING
FULL PROJECT EXAMPLE
visual.title: Agile Testing Real Project Case Study | Booking & Payments | Episode 12
visual.question: What evidence supports your release decision?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.text: We conclude with a fictional subscription appointment-booking platform containing a customer website, mobile app, admin dashboard and backend A P I services. Our fictional platform lets customers register, find appointments, reserve a slot, pay and receive confirmation. Staff use an administrative dashboard, while a mobile app and website share backend services. A customer sees one journey, but the system contains several boundaries where information can be delayed or misunderstood. We will build a connected testing plan across three illustrative sprints. The schedule is a teaching example, not a requirement that real teams deliver these exact features in separate sprints. Focus on how each increment adds evidence and how earlier checks continue protecting behavior as the product grows.

chapters.title: Requirements
chapters.text: The backlog includes registration, appointment discovery, booking, payments and notifications. Refinement uncovers risks involving duplicate bookings, payment failures, cancellations and authorization. Refine the journey before implementation. A reservation must belong to the requesting customer, a slot must not be confirmed for two people and a payment outcome must update the booking consistently. Ask when temporary holds expire, how cancellation affects availability and what happens if a notification arrives late. Identify dependencies among identity, availability and payment services. Translate the highest risks into examples that product, development and testing participants can understand. This prevents the team from treating five attractive screens as five independent features when their correctness actually depends on shared state and coordinated outcomes.

chapters.title: Sprint 1: Authentication
chapters.text: Developers implement registration and login. Tests cover valid and invalid input, duplicate accounts, password recovery and sessions. Concurrent registration exposes a race condition; the team fixes and retests it. In the first sprint, test registration and login with synthetic accounts. Check valid input, rejected input, duplicate addresses, recovery and session behavior. Now send two registration requests for the same address close together. A defect could allow duplicate accounts if the implementation checks availability and creates the record as separate unprotected steps. Record the observed outcome, discuss a safe implementation and retest the fix. Add an appropriate regression check. The important lesson is not a particular database command; it is that a realistic concurrency question can expose a defect that sequential happy-path checks miss.
chapters.direction: Registration API test and defect resolution.

chapters.title: Sprint 2: Booking
chapters.text: Tests cover available slots, unavailable slots, simultaneous booking and cancellation. Integration tests protect against double booking. Exploratory testing identifies confusing messages and prompts an improvement. In the booking increment, create one isolated appointment slot and two customers. Send competing reservation attempts. Under the agreed rule, exactly one should succeed and the stored booking must match the winning customer. Check the response for the unsuccessful customer and confirm that it offers an understandable next step. Cancel the successful reservation if the policy permits it, then verify whether availability returns as agreed. Also explore stale screens: a customer may select a slot that someone else reserved moments earlier. The interface and the backend must work together to handle that change safely.
chapters.direction: Two customers competing for one slot.

chapters.title: Sprint 3: Payments
chapters.text: Using a payment sandbox, test success, failure, cancellation, delayed confirmation and duplicate callbacks. A network timeout reveals incorrect payment-state handling. The team adds safe recovery and repeat-notification checks. For payments, stay in the provider's sandbox. Test success, decline, user cancellation, delayed confirmation and a repeated callback. Suppose the provider accepted payment but the platform lost the response. A retry should not create a second charge or second booking. Define the recovery policy and examine how unique request identifiers and payment-state transitions support it. Verify records as well as the displayed message. A page saying Payment failed while the provider recorded success is a serious inconsistency. Capture the evidence and add focused checks for the failure mode rather than relying only on the standard successful purchase journey.
chapters.direction: Payment state diagram and test results.

chapters.title: Regression and nonfunctional quality
chapters.text: Run regression checks across authentication, booking and payments. Evaluate performance under concurrent searches, authorization controls, accessibility and resilience. Document remaining risks. As new increments arrive, rerun relevant checks across identity, booking and payment. A permission change in the dashboard could affect existing customer access. A payment-state fix could accidentally prevent cancellation. Add nonfunctional questions where the risks justify them: concurrent search traffic, keyboard accessibility, account isolation and recovery after a dependency failure. Use realistic synthetic data and record the tested conditions. No single green pipeline proves complete readiness. Combine automated results with exploratory findings, unresolved defects and operational evidence to explain what is known and what uncertainty remains.

chapters.title: Release and monitoring
chapters.text: Review Definition of Done, outstanding defects, deployment and rollback plans. After release, monitor logs, failures and service health. Treat production feedback as another input to the quality cycle. Before release, inspect the shared quality conditions, open risks, deployment steps and recovery plan. Make sure relevant evidence belongs to the intended release candidate. If a serious unresolved payment issue remains, either resolve it or make an explicit scope and release decision with the responsible stakeholders. After deployment, monitor error signals, transaction consistency and customer feedback using appropriate access controls. A successful deployment command is not the end of quality work. Production observations can reveal conditions that the test environment did not reproduce, and those observations should inform both fixes and future checks.

chapters.title: Worked example
chapters.text: Your final exercise is to present a release recommendation for this platform. Name the three highest risks, give one piece of evidence for each and identify any remaining uncertainty. A strong response connects duplicate-registration checks, competing-booking results and payment-recovery verification to specific builds and conditions. It also explains how the team will detect problems after release. Look back at the whole course: principles guided priorities, methods shaped examples, artifacts preserved evidence, tools accelerated feedback and collaboration connected the work. You now have a practical way to discuss Agile Testing as part of delivering a product, from the first question through production learning.

chapters.title: A closer look
chapters.text: Trace one defect across the entire case study. A repeated payment notification creates two booking confirmations. Start by reproducing the sequence with synthetic data in the sandbox. Link the failure to the rule that one successful payment should confirm one reservation. Investigate how event identifiers and state transitions are handled. After the fix, repeat the original sequence, test a delayed notification and verify that a distinct legitimate payment still works. Retain the build and results. This evidence chain connects discovery, implementation and verification, giving the release discussion more substance than the statement that the ticket is now closed.

chapters.title: Verify the outcome
chapters.text: Finally, prepare a post-release learning loop. Identify which signals would reveal duplicate confirmations, unusual payment failures or growing booking errors. Agree who reviews those signals and how a new issue enters the team's work. Use operational data with the access and privacy controls appropriate to the product. When an incident occurs, examine the contributing conditions and improve both the product and the relevant checks. Production monitoring does not replace pre-release testing, and testing does not eliminate the need to observe a live service. Together they provide feedback across the product's life and help the team adapt when real usage reveals a new risk.

chapters.title: Course conclusion
chapters.text: Agile Testing begins with clear requirements and continues through development, integration, exploration, automation and production. Quality is shared across the team. Congratulations on completing the masterclass. Thank you for completing the Agile Testing Masterclass with Tech at sixty. Keep your examples and evidence, apply the approach to a small feature, and share your most useful takeaway in the comments. Subscribe for more practical software testing tutorials.
